verses.text: Hiram king of Tyre sent his servants to Solomon; for he had heard that they had anointed him king in the place of his father, and Hiram had always loved David.

“You know that David my father could not build a house for the name of Yahweh his God because of the wars which were around him on every side, until Yahweh put his enemies under the soles of his feet.
But now Yahweh my God has given me rest on every side. There is no enemy and no evil occurrence.

Behold, I intend to build a house for the name of Yahweh my God, as Yahweh spoke to David my father, saying, ‘Your son, whom I will set on your throne in your place shall build the house for my name.’

Now therefore command that cedar trees be cut for me out of Lebanon. My servants will be with your servants; and I will give you wages for your servants according to all that you say. For you know that there is nobody among us who knows how to cut timber like the Sidonians.”
When Hiram heard the words of Solomon, he rejoiced greatly, and said, “Blessed is Yahweh today, who has given to David a wise son to rule over this great people.”
Hiram sent to Solomon, saying, “I have heard the message which you have sent to me. I will do all your desire concerning timber of cedar, and concerning cypress timber.

My servants will bring them down from Lebanon to the sea. I will make them into rafts to go by sea to the place that you specify to me, and will cause them to be broken up there, and you will receive them. You will accomplish my desire, in giving food for my household.”
So Hiram gave Solomon cedar timber and cypress timber according to all his desire.
Solomon gave Hiram twenty thousand cors  of wheat for food to his household, and twenty cors  of pure oil. Solomon gave this to Hiram year by year.
Yahweh gave Solomon wisdom, as he promised him. There was peace between Hiram and Solomon, and the two of them made a treaty together.
King Solomon raised a levy out of all Israel; and the levy was thirty thousand men.
He sent them to Lebanon, ten thousand a month by courses; for a month they were in Lebanon, and two months at home; and Adoniram was over the men subject to forced labor.
Solomon had seventy thousand who bore burdens, and eighty thousand who were stone cutters in the mountains;
besides Solomon’s chief officers who were over the work, three thousand and three hundred, who ruled over the people who labored in the work.
The king commanded, and they cut out large stones, costly stones, to lay the foundation of the house with worked stone.
Solomon’s builders and Hiram’s builders and the Gebalites cut them, and prepared the timber and the stones to build the house.

footnotes.content: Hiram's love for David carries forward to his son. A good reputation grows like cedar roots—deep and outlasting the man who planted it. Notice how Hiram moves first toward blessing: he hears Solomon is king and reaches out in friendship, not suspicion.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon answers with a message, not a demand. He meets Hiram as one builder to another, even before asking for help. This is how the Lord's work begins—with clarity about what we're really building.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David could not build because of wars—the plain reality. Solomon names it directly, without complaint. Sometimes God asks us to wait. The house of God was not David's to build, though it burned in his heart. Rest comes when the Lord decides, not when we think we're ready.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now Yahweh has given Solomon rest on every side. Peace is not mere absence of war—it's the space where the Lord's work can unfold. Solomon recognizes this rest as a gift, not an achievement. In that gift-space, he can build.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon remembers a word spoken to his father long ago: *Your son shall build the house for my name.* He holds that promise lightly and humbly—not boasting, but stating what he knows to be true. A son who builds what his father's heart desired honors both his father and his God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon asks Hiram to command that cedar be cut. He doesn't demand; he requests with respect and offers fair wages. He knows what he doesn't know—the Sidonians know cedar as he does not—and he says so plainly. This is the beginning of wisdom: knowing your need and asking humbly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hiram hears these words and rejoices greatly. He blesses the Lord and speaks of Solomon's wisdom with joy. Not envy, not hesitation—pure gladness that a wise son rules and builds. This is how brothers in the Lord grieve or rejoice: Hiram sees God's hand in Solomon.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hiram's answer is swift and generous: I will do all your desire. He has heard Solomon's humble request and answers with abundance. When the Lord opens a door, His servants walk through it together—not as masters and slaves, but as partners in His purpose.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hiram's servants will bring cedar down from Lebanon, lash it into rafts, and float it by sea. He shows the whole picture—from the mountain to Solomon's hand—and asks only that Solomon provide food for Hiram's household. Work and sustenance flow both ways.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: So Hiram gave Solomon cedar and cypress according to all his desire. The transaction unfolds simply, without greed or trickery. Two kings, two nations—bound by honest dealing and the Lord's purpose—become instruments of His work.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon gives Hiram wheat and pure oil, year by year. The covenant is not one-time; it is sustained and faithful. Both men are givers. Hiram gives trees; Solomon gives bread and oil. The Lord loves a cheerful giver—and so do the nations.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh gave Solomon wisdom, as he promised him. Peace and treaty flow from that wisdom. When the Lord gives wisdom, He gives also the fruit of wisdom—peace between former strangers, trust where suspicion might have lived. This is not luck; it is the work of the Spirit.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: King Solomon raised a levy of thirty thousand men from all Israel. The whole nation gathers to build what David could not. Each man is called to a season of labor—not for Solomon's glory, but for the house of the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ten thousand a month, by course: a month in Lebanon, two months at home. Solomon orders the labor so that no man is crushed by endless toil. He sees them as men with homes and families, not as tools. Even kings can show mercy in the ordering of work.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seventy thousand bearers of burdens, eighty thousand stone cutters in the mountains. Vast numbers—but each a man. Each has skill, sweat, a name. The house of God is built on the labor of thousands whom Solomon will never know by name, yet whom he must remember.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three thousand three hundred chiefs oversee the work. Even the overseers need overseers. Good government sees that leaders serve the workers, not the other way around. The Lord's house is built by order and justice, not chaos.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Large stones, costly stones, worked with care—the foundation must be worthy. The Lord sees what no eye will see once the house stands: the faithfulness of those who lay what is hidden. Readers today hear an echo in this: we lay foundations no one praises, trusting the Lord sees.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon's builders and Hiram's builders and the Gebalites cut and prepared timber and stone together. Men of three nations—all strangers once—now work as one. The Lord's house draws together what the world divides. That is its power.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
